sn1.13:2.2: Vājasaneyi Saṁhitā 23.48b says cattle have no measure.
sn1.13:2.3: These lines closely mirror the question at Vājasaneyi Saṁhitā 23.47a (quoted at Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 13.5.2.13), “What light equals the sun? What lake equals the ocean?” The answers given in the next verse are “Brahmā” and “heaven”. This points to the myth that the rivers, especially the Ganges, originate in the “causal ocean” (_garbhodaka_) of heaven. The rivers of northern India, bringing life down from the Himalayas, naturally suggest a divine origin.
sn1.13:2.4: _Sara_ means originally “flow”, hence “stream, river”, then “lake”. The ocean as the paramount lake is a destination, the final point where rivers converge. As such it evokes the Upaniṣadic idea that consciousness converges in Divinity (see notes on [sn1.61:2.4]() and [mn9:53.2]()). This is ultimately the same as the “causal ocean” from which the rivers flow.
sn1.13:3.1: The Theravada tradition, starting from the Vimuttimagga, begins the  meditation on love (_mettā_) by focusing on oneself, a practice that draws on passages such as this. See also [sn3.8](), [ud5.1](). Here the Pali uses _pema_ (“fondness”) rather than _mettā_ (“love”).
sn1.13:3.4: By pointing to the rain, the Buddha indicates the natural cause of the lakes and oceans.
